newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels to accept only limited intervention.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels to accept only limited intervention.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Saturday he had told the Canadian commander of a planned intervention force for eastern Zaire that only a handful of foreign soldiers could enter the region.

He was speaking at a news conference in the looted palace of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko at Himbi, on the outskirts of Goma. He met Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, commander of the force intended to help feed refugees, in the palace on Thursday.
"We agreed that they can only send a small group of soldiers, not more than five, who would be specialists. Their duties would be to coordinate airdrops," Kabila said.

"But they cannot drop food, because it will feed the enemy," he said, sitting on a pink and gold striped sofa. "We will allow them to drop food if we are informed of a big concentration of refugees, but it is a stupid idea."

The force now has a forward headquarters, in the Ugandan capital of Kampala, but the countries involved, led by Canada, have still not decided whether to go ahead with airdrops or try to take food to the refugees in eastern Zaire by road.
The rebels deny there are large numbers of refugees left to feed, and Kabila said military intervention was politically motivated, "a pretext to assist the ruler of this country".
He said there were "no refugees between Fizi and Bukavu, and I think the problem of refugees is over in this area".

Kabila also gave details of towns which he said the rebels now held, including Butembo and Lubero to the north of Goma, but he said Walikale, about 150 km (90 miles) to the west of Goma, was "giving us problems".

He said the rebels had received reports that the Interahamwe (Rwandan Hutu militias) and Zairean army troops were looting, killing and raping, "and the local population has asked us to come in". There were also reports of a pocket of Interahamwe in the Virunga National Park, he said.
Kabila said that Mai-Mai militias -- local warriors who practise witchcraft -- were being actively recruited. "But they are without discipline and must be politicised and trained," he said.
Before the news conference, Kabila met local authorities and businessmen to discuss security and the economy.
"We are doing what we can, but the pylon blown up by the Interahamwe is still down, so there is no electricity and water in Goma," he said.

At Sake, between 2,000 and 3,000 refugees who had slept overnight at the side of the road were taken by truck to Goma in a convoy of 20 UNHCR vehicles from Rwanda, and more refugees continued to arrive from the direction of Minova.
